title: 'Cruel and Unlawful': Family of ICU Nurse Killed by Federal Agents Accuses DOJ of Stonewalling
snippet: The parents of Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old nurse shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis, are demanding transparency as state officials sue the Department of Justice over blocked evidence.
content:
MINNEAPOLIS — The heartbroken parents of Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse shot and killed by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis earlier this year, are breaking their silence to accuse the Department of Justice of unlawfully stonewalling their search for truth and justice.

Speaking at a news conference on Tuesday, Michael and Susan Pretti slammed federal authorities for refusing to provide substantive updates or share key investigative files with local law enforcement, effectively shielding the agents responsible for their son's death.

"We will no longer stay silent about the actions of the Department of Justice in the 275 days since Alex's murder," Michael Pretti said during the family's first public press briefing since the fatal January encounter.

A Broken Promise of Transparency

According to an exclusive letter sent to Attorney General Todd Blanche in July, the family's attorney, Steve Schleicher, stated that the DOJ has violated federal victims' rights laws through an ongoing pattern of secrecy. In the missive, Schleicher described the federal government's posture toward the grieving family as "cruel," "unconscionable," and "unlawful."

During a July meeting with U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota Dan Rosen, the family sought basic answers regarding the investigation. However, Rosen reportedly refused to provide any details, citing unnamed restrictions without giving a legal basis.

"I've never seen a family treated with such cruelty and disrespect," Schleicher said on Tuesday, adding that the DOJ has ignored follow-up inquiries.

Federal Blockade Prompts Legal Battle

The Pretti family's fight highlights a broader standoff between local Minnesota prosecutors and federal officials. While state and federal law enforcement initially reached an evidence-sharing agreement over the summer, the DOJ abruptly halted cooperation weeks later.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is currently pursuing litigation against the Department of Justice to force the release of the complete case file, including ballistics evidence from the weapons fired that day. Local authorities note that federal agents initially blocked state investigators from accessing the crime scene entirely until a state judge intervened.

"Any prosecutor can tell you, you can't go forward with half a file. You need the whole thing," Ellison told CNN on Tuesday morning. In court filings, the DOJ argued it is under no legal obligation to turn over evidence to state authorities prior to active state court proceedings.

Contradictory Narratives and Video Proof

Pretti's death occurred during Operation Metro Surge, an aggressive federal immigration sweep that sparked nationwide protests following multiple fatal shootings. Initial statements from top officials depicted Pretti as an violent aggressor; former DHS leadership labeled him a "terrorist," while White House aides branded him an "assassin."

However, bystander video footage directly contradicted those claims. The footage shows Pretti being pepper-sprayed during a chaotic encounter on a Minneapolis street. Video records confirm that an agent disarmed Pretti—removing a handgun from his waistband and stepping away—seconds before multiple officers opened fire, unleashing a barrage of at least 10 gunshots into the disoriented nurse.

"No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex," Michael Pretti recalled bitterly.

A Legacy Beyond the Headlines

Appearing later on CNN's The Lead with Jake Tapper, Susan Pretti shared how deeply her son was loved by his hospital colleagues and former patients, describing the outpouring of support as a comforting reminder of his life's work.

"No parent should have to live what we're living," Susan Pretti said. "What the federal government has taken away from us, from his friends, his family, his colleagues, from his patients... it's reprehensible."

The family's legal team has demanded that the DOJ publicly identify the agents who fired the fatal shots, resume full cooperation with Minnesota prosecutors, and return Pretti's personal belongings. While the family has not yet filed a civil lawsuit, Schleicher emphasized that they reserve all legal avenues to ensure full accountability.
